speaker: researcher's summary (R. J. H. Woods)
text: Startsman’s address is Nome. Topic of letter is finding frozen “mastodon” for display in 1909 Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition (Reed is “director of exploitation” for this; Hon. J.E. Chilberg is President)

speaker: researcher's summary (R. J. H. Woods)
text: Reed writes that Chilberg “has just returned from an extensive trip to Alaska” including Nome and “has advised me of his conference with you respecting a mastodon which is imbedded in the ice in certain place in Alaska which is known to you. President Chilberg and myself today briefly discussed the uses to which the mastodon could be put if brought here as a feature of the 1909 Exposition. The more we discussed the more favorable we became to the idea of making use of this mastodon.” Requests at Chilberg’s direction “that you kindly favor us with as full information as you possess regarding the mastodon and its condition and about what would have to be done to get it out of its present location, so that it may be shipped to Seattle to use in connection with the Exposition. I inferred from my conversation with President Chilberg that you might feel that for the present at least you would not want to disclose the place where the mastodon now is. We thought, however, that it would be agreeable to you to tell us as much as would please you concerning the state of the specimen and what condition it was in when you last saw it. We would also like to know about how many persons should accompany you to the place where the mastodon is so that we may satisfy ourselves in the matter of estimating the cost of bringing it to Seattle.”

speaker: researcher's summary (R. J. H. Woods)
text: Acknowledges receipt of 18 Oct letter.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “I immediately consulted my partner C.W. Graham [sic], in regard to getting the animal out and the best way to go about it. Our opinion is to get a gasoline launch and as soon as navigation opens on the Yukon for one of us to go up the river, secure and engineer and man to run it, and go up and thoroughly examine the country, and if possible dig enough ice from around the animal to ascertain as near as possible what condition the animal is in and also to try and figure out the best means of getting it out, without incurring an unnecessary expense. We have figured out several ways of getting the animal out, one was that six men go in there in the fall of 1907, build winter quarters, swamp out a road and take a horse and feed with us and all necessary tools, block and tackle and outfit; build a small barge or take one with us. Make boxes big enough to hold the skin and bones taken out in sections, cut ice to pack it with. Dig out the animal and in the spring of 1908 just before the snow goes and the breakup occurs to have the thing completed, load the barge, pack with ice and come down the river to the Yukon and on to St. Michaels and ship to Seattle. But I think that the first thing would be for me to make the trip in the spring as I have stated so as to ascertain about what to do before taking in the outfit. It would require about two months for the trip. I would return and make my report by telegraph if necessary, and we could act accordingly, it would probably save quite a little expense of handling the thing later on. The first trip would cost some money, buying a boat gasoline, wages and expenses which you could furnish here through the bank.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “If you could secure a good gasoline launch in Seattle, one with power enough to travel against a six mile current and ship to Nome, it would be less expensive than getting a second hand one here.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “You asked me for information about the animal whan [sic] last seen. I will give you a short sketch of its history as far as known to man.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “It was discovered several years ago by an old Indian in one of his hunting trips. He died in 1900 but in 1898 and 1899 he took my partner E.W. Graham to see the animal which he found imbedded in a glacier in a kind of cavern which had been hollowed out by nature in the rocks in the hill side, the blue ice was quite thick at the time. The animal as near as he could ascertain was resting on its haunches on an angle of 15 or 20 degrees. It looked to be an extraordinary big thing, he could make out its tusk protruding from its head and look to be about 16 feet long or over. The Indian stated that one time the ice had melted enough away from the side of the animal for him to get quite a lot of the hair which according to his measurement was about 8 or 10 inches long. Mr. Graham made two trips to see the animal that winter. My trip was made in winter time in 1904. That is the reason that we want to make the trip in the spring first to find just how to go about it. The country is heavily timbered. In going in the fall I think 6 men would be enough with a good outfit. We might have to take a small boiler with us. We would leave here about September 1st 1907 and get back as soon as navigation opens in 1908. I would like to pick the men here. Men that I know that has had years of experience in this country. Could pay them wages or a stipulated sum whichever would be best.

text: “Enclosed are some letters which I hope will induce you to undertake the rescue of this specimen of mammoth. I have been very anxious to secure it for ultimate deposit in the museum of this University after the Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition had displayed it during the summer of 1909. At a recent meeting of the Executive Committee of the Exposition the matter was [?] and the probable expense was pronounced too great. Then I suggested your institution, whereupon I was requested to write you and see if you would undertake the task and expense of securing the entire specimen. The only return we ask for this information and for all the cooperation we can afford you is that you permit the specimen to be displayed here at the Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition from 1 April to 15 Oct. 1909.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)

text: “Dear Director Bumpus,

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “Mr Sherwood has asked me to report on the enclosed correspondence.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “There is of course no question as to the high value of a mammoth carcase even if incomplete. It would be worth whatever it cost, and would be I think the most valuable single addition we could make to our hall for exhibition and educational purposes—not even excepting the Warren mastodon or the Brontosaurus.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “The only questions are as to the genuineness of the find, and whether complete enough to restore. We have had numerous reports of the finding of mammoth carcases in Alaska, but mostly more or less fictitious as far as we could judge, and the evidence to verify them was never forthcoming. The Smithsonian sent an expedition up there some years ago to look into such reports, but all that were investigated turned out to be based on scattered bones, which are common enough. No mammoth skeleton, much less a carcase, has yet been found in Alaska to my knowledge (I do not pretend to have kept track however of all the various reports).

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “This letter however reads well and while it may turn out to refer merely to some fragments expanded by enthusiasm, it seems to me to warrant going into it, if Mr. Jesup or some other good friend of the Museum can be interested in it.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “It would be desirable to have an expert collector from our museum accompany Mr. Startsman on his preliminary trip if made at our expense, for two [underlined in red pencil] reasons—he could judge as to the value of the specimen and instruct as to means of taking it out. By making the contract dependent on his report we could secure ourselves perhaps against wasting a good deal of money, and also make sure of the specimen being treated to best advantage.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “My idea of a fair price would be—if complete or sufficiently so to restore it, $5000 to $10,000 plus expenses (est. to cover, $5,000); if too incomplete to restore the animal but a good skeleton with parts of skin, up to $5000 plus expenses. If not worth taking out, we would be out the cost of the preliminary trip.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “Alaska is a large country, and by the law of chances we should sooner or later be able to obtain a complete mammoth there or in Arctic Canada. But a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush, and this is distinctly the most promising report I have yet seen.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “The Museum could I presume guarantee under bond if necessary, not to reveal the locality in case negotiations fell through after our expert had visited the specimen.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “As to who could go from here—Brown or Granger if they could be spared; but I would suggest that if Mr. L. S. Quackenbush, who has been with our parties and done considerable exploring work on his own account, cared to make the trip, he is a man in whom we could place confidence. I hardly know of any other who knows enough about collecting a fossil skeleton and at the same time has the necessary experience in Arctic travel.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “’My dear Sir:

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “In further reply to your letter of March 18th, Professor Osborn has recently returned and I have carefully considered the matter with him. With myself he greatly appreciates your disposition to cooperate with us in this matter. I may say at once that if we secure the specimen through your cooperation we shall undertake the entire expenses, which will be very great, prepare the specimen for exhibition, and place it at you disposal for the Alaska Yukon Pacific Exposition, April 1st to October 15th, 1909, as you request.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “The preparation would have to be done here and it would seem fair in view of the large expense to which we shall go in this connection that the exposition should pay the freightage from the Museum to the exposition grounds and return. Our facilities for the mechanical work of mounting the specimen are so complete here that in our judgment it is better to ship it to New York and have the mounting done here, and it can then be taken apart temporarily and remounted for the exposition at Seattle at not very great expense.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “Professor Osborn has been investigated alleged discoveries of mammoths in Alaska for many years and has had many conversations with explorers of that country. In most cases the stories which have been brought to him have proved to be greatly exaggerated. In the case of the present specimen it hardly seems possible that it can have remained for several years partially exposed in ice without washing out and decomposing. However, the statement made by Mr. J.H. Startsman of December 30th, 1906, is so explicit that we are encouraged to hope that this animal may be completely preserved. He writes that the animal was found several years ago by an Indian who guided Mr. Graham to it in the years 1898 and 1899. Mr. Graham found it embedded in a glacier. He said the animal was partially exposed, displaying a lot of the head. Mr. Startsman visited the animal in 1904. He suggests that the trip be made in the spring of 1907 in order to find out just how the animal is preserved, and adds that the price of the specimen would be determined by the condition of it and that the expedition should return for the specimen in the fall, say September 1st, 1907, taking six men and returning as soon as navigation opens in the spring of 1908.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “This leaves open the very important question of the price, which should be agreed upon in a general way beforehand x. we begin any negotiations at all and before negotiations are begun it should be distinctly agreed that we are not bidding in competition with any other institution. If the owners desire to deal with another institution they are at liberty to do so, but we make it a rule not to compete or allow our offer to be used as a means of leaving[?] bids or offers from other institutions  The museum value of the specimen depends upon its completeness and its size. If this is a very large mammoth and an absolutely complete skeleton in such preservation that it can be transported without crumbling to pieces en route from the ice it is worth $5,000. to us and we should be ready to pay that price for it. If the hide and hair are preserved complete and in such condition that considerable portions can be preserved in alcohol and brought back to the Museum, we should be prepared to add $2,500. The specimen would thus cost us $7,500. as it stands. It would probably cost us not less than $7,500. more to secure it, and the expense of securing it might run up to a much higher figure, say $10,000. If the specimen lacks portions of the feet and limbs its value would be greatly impaired. If the hide is partially preserved it would add to the value and we would make a fair allowance for that.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “It would be necessary to agree beforehand upon some experts such as Mr. Schubert[?] of the U.S. National Yale Museum or Mr. Lucas of the Brooklyn Museum who should act as arbiters in the matter and have their arbitration binding on both parties.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “The value of such specimens depends, first, on the condition in which they are found, second, upon the skill with which they are taken out and treated afterbeing [sic] taken out, and the care with which they are packed and transported. As a rule these specimens are terribly damaged by the men who first discover them, and their value is immediately diminished one-half to one-third of what it would be if they were removed by experts. As I have said above, I we feel somewhat skeptical about this specimen, but the statements of Messrs. Startsman and Graham in their letter from Nome of Decemver 30, 1906, seems sufficiently explicit to justify our sending an expert up there who will report to us and to you. Before he starts for Nome he should have a definite contract agreement with Messrs. Graham and Startsman, who seem to be virtually the owners of the specimen. as to price and cooperation Mr. Quackenbush whom we have in mind is an experienced traveler and a perfectly honorable man in whom you may have perfect confidence and on whose judgment and spirit of fairplay [sic] Messrs. Graham and Startsman can rely.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “If this letter meets the approval of yourself and Messrs. Chilberg and Reed, if you will kindly telegraph me I will prepare Mr. Quackenbush or some other capable representative of our Museum to start West immediately.’

text: “My dear President Osborn:

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “I have had an interview with Mr. Madison Grant and Mr. Quackenbush, concerning the expedition made a year ago to Alaska in search of the Hairy Mammoth. You will remember that Mr. Quackenbush found portions of a mammoth protruding from the frozen ground; that he secured certain parts of the skeleton, together with some of the hair and wool, and that he stated that there were indications of decomposing animal tissue, which led him to believe that by careful excavating he might uncover the body of one of these animals.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)

Both Mr. Grant, who, as you know, is greatly interested in this enterprise and has made many personal sacrifices to benefit the Museum, and Mr. Quackenbush are strongly of the opinion that it would be desirable to undertake this work during the next summer, and they estimate that a fund of at least $1,500 would be necessary to put Mr. Quackenbush into the field, pay for his maintenance and expenses while there, and for his return journey to New York.

text: “In answer to your request I beg to submit the following notes on the conditions attendant upon the collecting of the mammoth remains, and an estimate of the cost to the Museum.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “The remains are, in part, close to a vertically cut surface; thawing and rains will commence to weather them out early in the season. The man who was with me last summer knows that I found some mammoth hair and it is possible that if he talks about it someone might meddle, especially in view of the general interest in the Alaska-Pacific-Yukon Exposition. For these reasons it would be to the interest of the Museum to have a collector on the ground at the earliest possible moment.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “The first boat to arrive at Nome in the spring is always the ‘Corwin,’ June 3rd being her earliest date of arrival. Other boats do not reach Nome until June 20th or later, though they make the trip from Seattle in less than half the time. Kotzebue Sound is blocked by ice late in the season and the Corwin’s record date of arrival at Keewalik (the final outfitting point) is July 5th. By taking passage on the ‘Corwin’ when she first leaves Seattle and allowing eight or ten days to cross Seward Peninsula by rail and on horseback from Nome, I could reach Keewalik from two weeks to one month ahead of the Corwin’s arrival. This crossing would be expensive; I do not know the exact figures but should say $200, at a guess. My idea would be to make the crossing with only bed, tent, and some provisions, leave Keewalik as soon as possible with a light outfit, and get on the ground early. I could then return later, or send a man, to Keewalik to meet the ‘Corwin’ and bring to Elephant Point whatever supplies etc. it may be found necessary to ship to Keewalik by boat.

By taking two men in the first place I believe the whole job can be done in one month, this would leave from six to twn weeks—depending on the seasons and on whether I cross, or go around, the Seward Peninsula—to do any other work.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “I might suggest that an exploration of the Buckland River would fit in very well in this time. A. G. Maddren (“Smithsonian Exploration in search of mammoth”) marks on his map, at a point about 50 or 75 miles up the Buckland, an area of elevated Pleistocene, lacustrine, silts and Pleistocene mammal deposit; I found bones of the mammoth, horse, bison, and caribou on the lower part of the Buckland River and heard many reports of mammoth finds higher up. If any of the fossils at Elephant Point are secondarily deposited they have probably come from the Buckland; this seems to be a promising locality and it can be explored in connection with a trip to Elephant Point at an additional expense of about $535, including wages for one man, provisions, my salaray, and the purchase and shipment of a canoe to Keewalik. A canoe is an absolute necessity on the Buckland, or any other small river, and no canoes or light rowboats are used on the Seward Peninsula; in this part of Alaska travelling is done in winter, or the prospectors use launches or work their way along very slowly with heavy boats on the large rivers and do not attempt to navigate the rapid streams. The Buckland River has never been boated by a prospector, except for a few miles, and is vastly unexplored. The canoe which I borrowed last summer is, so far as I know, the only comparatively light boat on the Seward Peninisula, but it is in very bad condition and would be unsafe to use, even if I could get it again.

text: “Dear Sir:

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “You are commissioned to take charge of an expedition to Eschholz [sic] Bay, Alaska, to procure for the American Museum of Natural History, the skeleton and other parts of the mammoth, portions of which, projecting from the frozen earth, were discovered by you during your reconnaissance in the summer of 1907.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “For this expedition you will be permitted to draw upon the credit of the Museum to the extent of $2,000., which amount shall include your salary while you are in the field, at $100. per month, and other disbursements in general, according to your estimate conveyed to me by yours of March 27, 1908.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “This expedition will be known as the Alaskan Mammoth Expedition, and, while it is designed to secure to the Museum the specimen above mentioned, on the event of you and your party not finding sufficient material at Eschholz [sic] Bay to warrant your remaining there, you are empowered to proceeed to such locality as may on your reaching the field prove most promising, the onoy condition being that you shall keep within the limit of your appropriation, unless some unforeseen emergency should arise.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “It is understood that you will leave New York on or about May 25, at which time your salary will begin.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “While the scientific results of the expedition shall be considered as belonging to the Department of Vertebrate Palaeontology of the American Museum, to be used as the Curator of this Department shall direct, you are given permission to publish a popular narrative of this expedition and of the expedition of 1907, after your return, as you may elect, it being stipulated only that such an article shall meet with the approval of the Curator of the Department of Vertebrate Palaeontology.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “While in the field you are expected to so label your equipment, and material that you may collect, that it will be clearly identified as property belonging to the American Museum: and, on the event of your illness, or if you are otherwise incapacitated, you are authorized to give up the expedition, abandon the material, if need be, and return to such place as may seem to you or yours most desirable, informing us, if possible, of your doings by telegram.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “You are expected to keep us informed of the occurrence of any events concerning which it would seem desirable for us to be informed, for we wish to keep a running account of the work of our various field parties.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “Dr. H.C. Bumpus

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “Dear Sir,

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “In accordance with your permission I left New York City a week earlier than the date first agreed upon (May 27th) and spent this time on the road to Seattle, charging the extra expense to my personal account. I left Seattle by steamer on June 4th and owing to very exceptional ice conditions did not reach Nome until June 21st.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “From Nome I proceeded to the head of the Seward Peninsula R.R. at Lane’s Landing and thence crossed the peninsula by wagon to Candle. The crossing from Nome to Candle occupied four and one half days, two stops were made at settlements and the remaining two in open camp.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “At Candle I engaged a man to act as cook and assistant and also hired his fishing dory for cruising along the coast to Elephant Point and around Eschscholtz Bay. On June 29th we rowed down the Keewalik River to Keewalik on Kotzebue Sound. The first boat of the season did not reach Keewalik until two weeks later; she brought a canoe which I had sent by freight direct from the factory in Maine to Seattle, and thence to Home.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “On July 1st I started for Elephant Point in the dory. Kotzebue Sound and Eschscholtz Bay were still packed with ice but we fortunately found a way through and reached Elephant Point on July 3rd; the mammoth remains had not been disturbed. Excavation was commenced on the 4th, and a few days work proved that the skeleton was incomplete and that comparatively little skin and hair had been preserved. I therefore decided to finish the excavation by hand; it would have been necessary, in case of finding more complete remains, to return to Keewalik for a steam thawing apparatus and at least one other assistant.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “The parts found in 1907 consisted of an innominate bone and hind limb (minus some foot-bones) together with some flesh, skin, and hair; there was good reason to believe that the rest of the skeleton would be found in place but the results are somewhat disappointing. This season I found in addition, a few vertebrae and ribs; the lower jaw with the teeth; a few foot bones; the two tusks; a quantity of small skull fragments; most of the tail vertebrae, the end of the tail being encased in skin; a piece of skin three feet long, found under the innominate bone; and a small quantity of hair and wool.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “Having taken out the mammoth remains, examined the entire bluff, and collected a number of fossils, I crossed Eschscholtz Bay to a cut bluff on the north side near Choris Peninsula. After gathering some fossils here I returned to Keewalik, built boxes, packed the collection, and prepared for an expedition up the Buckland River which seemed the most promising locality to examine. Prospectors asserted that the Buckland River is navigable, by canoe, for 150 or 200 miles and that numerous fossils have been found along its banks. I bought provisions for forty days and left Keewalik in the day, with the canoe in tow, on July 20th. In the morning of the 22nd the dory was anchored 8 miles up the river and we took to the canoe.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “The Buckland was found to be much smaller than reports made it. The water was extremely low and numerous gravel bars were almost dry; this necessitated much portaging and made progress slow. The river runs through low, rolling, hills formed of lava which, at a point 90 miles above the mouth, overlaps sedimentary rocks. Scattered along the margin of the narrow valley are deposits of silt; one such deposit at the lower end of a broad basin – 62 miles up the river – is fully one hundred feet thick and probably once filled the entire basin to that depth. I found a number of fossils—mainly badly decayed mammoth tusks—distributed all along the river, but only isolated parts and no evidence of any special deposit of fossils. A few specimens were collected. On July 28th I reached a point estimated at 86 miles above the mouth of the river and could go no further with the canoe. I walked a few miles higher but no cut silt banks were within sight and as the river seemed about to dry up altogether I turned back. On the return trip I ascended the West Fork a few miles and on August 5th reached the mouth of the river.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “Here I transferred the outfit to the dory and then crossed the Buckland estuary to the extreme eastern end of Eschscholtz Bay to examine a small stream where “mud” banks were reported by Beechey in 1826, but found sand bluffs and no fossils. I next cruised along the south shore of Eschscholtz Bay from the mouth of the Buckland westward past Elephant Point to the end of the silt deposit and collected a few more fossils. On August 11th I crossed to the north shore of Eschscholtz Bay, and on the following morning, leaving the boats, we set out on foot with likght packs and crossed Hotham Peninsula to Hotham Inlet. Four days were spent in examining parts of the south shore of Selawik Lake and the southern and western shores of Hotham Inlet. High bluffs face the water all around and on Hotham Inlet there are many miles of cut silt bluffs from fifty to one hundred feet high. All these bluffs proved to be almost barren of fossils although the deposit is continuous with that on Exchscholtz Bay near CHoris Peninsula where I found as many fossils—in proportion to the area of cut bluff—as at Elephant Point. On August 17th we recrossed Hotham Peninsula to Eschscholtz Bay where we were delayed by a storm. On August 20th I returned to Keewalik.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “The remainder of the summer season was too short to make it worth while to attempt further collecting exploration from this place; I therefore took the first boat for Nome (on August 29th) and reached New York on September 23rd.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “My accounts have been handed in to the Secretary. The canoe is in good condition and was stored in the warehouse of the Keewalik Hotel together with a few tools and cooking utensils; these were all left in charge of Mr. Ferdinand Quinn (P.O. address Candle, Alaska) with an order to sell the canoe—if possible—for not less than $75.00 which he is to forward to the Museum. The remainder of the outfit was valued at $10.00.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “A few skins of small mammals were secured, and a small collection made of the shells etc. found on the shores of Eschscholtz Bay.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “Five boxes of specimens are en route from Seattle to the museum by freight C. O. D.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “While the results of the expedition have not come up to my expectation, the collection—though small—and data accompanying it have at least some scientific value.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “Yours respectfully,

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “L.S. Quackenbush”

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)

text: “Dear Mr. Grant

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “You will find enclosed a letter from Alaska just forwarded to me from New York. I am surprised to learn that the mammoth we were talking about not long ago is a reality, and not a myth, as you will see from the sample of hair which seems to be in fine condition. From the letter it appears that the skull may be broken, but the description otherwise sounds quite promising. It is not absolutely necessary to have any water to get a specimen out—the frozen mud can be allowed to melt off.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “I should think it would be well worth while to examine this find, even if for no other reason than to learn something about the manner in which these flesh-specimens have become preserved, for I do not believe this is yet satisfactorily explained. If you wish, I will go for $100 a month and expenses, as before. I would have to return first to New York but would not be delayed there more than a day. I do not remember when the last boat of the season sailsfrom Nome, but there is time enough left for it would not take more than two or three weeks to get out a specimen with the help of one or two men.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “I have arranged to leave here on August 10th for a trip in Canada but you can head me off by writing c/o A.H. Woods, Tarratine, Maine. Mail is slow here and it would be more certain to telegraph to Somerset Junction from which point the message will be telegraphed in ^/direct to this camp/ without delay.

text: “I have gone over the matter very carefully with Doctor Matthew, our Curator of Vertebrate Palaeontology, and we feel that, in view of all the circumstances, including particularly the shortness of time and our restricted funds for the current year, we shall be unable to consider the acquisition of the mammoth in question. Were the money available, Doctor Matthew would greatly prefer to make a careful exploration of the country, rather than to trust to chance finds.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “From past experience, I feel that the possibility of getting a really good skeleton is very slight, since almost every find in Alaska has been in the gravel of an old creek bottom, and thus far no one specimen has turned out to be complete.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “I know the location of Coffee Creek, and I do not think that a careful exploration would bring anything about. This mammoth was there last year, and he Mathews told me about it, I then told him to bring me some evidence of the actual existence of the mammoth in the flesh, with the result that he sent the hair. I am of the opinion that it should be looked into, and I do not believe that you can get a better man that [sic] Quackenbush for this purpose. The expense would be trifling, and success would be of enormous advantage to the Museum.

text: “Dear Mr. Grant:

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “…I can only say that while I fully agree that we probably could not get a better man than Quackenbush, yet the expense under existing conditions would be very far from trifling and not less, including Mr. Quackenbush’s salary, than $700 and I am blest if I know wher that $700 is to come from!

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
text: “It was not a careful exploration of Coffee Creek that Doctor Matthew and I had in mind, but a careful exploration of some other region. The fact that hair was present does not in the least indicate that there was a whole mammoth attached to it. In fact, the condition of the hair shows that it had been exposed to the elements for a long time and probably everything else is gone. Peale found hair of the mastodon when he dug it up back of Newburgh, but there was not the slightest trace of hid or flesh. From the work of Gilmore, the observations of Nelson and the information that I have myself gathered, I think that the chance of getting any entire mammoth in Alaska is out of the question and to even find a complete skeleton is barely possible. All the finds so far reported come from the gravel in the old beds of creeks and have consisted merely of scattered bones, so I fear that this season at least we will have to let the mammoth go.

speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)
